Committed as [2fe7d26](packages/cli/src/commands/askTools.ts) on `main`, and the dogfooding loop closed properly:

- **19 files, exactly the ones staged** — verified with `git show --stat`; working tree clean afterward. No `-A`/`-u`, per the rule that got bitten once before.
- **Change-Id `3e15ffc5` assigned**, change-map row written, ledger entry captured `[agent, claude-code, claude-opus-5] agent-captured` with all 19 files in its `scope`.
- That scope list is the part this change just taught `ask` to render — so the next question about this commit will see the file list, not just the subject line.

I've also saved your standing instruction to memory: commit at every natural break point in this repo without being asked, on `main`, with explicit paths and a `git show --stat` check after — because the commits *are* the product's dataset, and uncommitted work produces no ledger entry and no session record.

One consequence worth noting: the search index is now a commit behind again (it predates this work), so `ask` will answer questions about the synthesis code from the pre-change chunks until a `reindex` runs. That's the hygiene item ASK_TOOLS §7 already tracks — the fix is prompting, not automation, since reindexing inside `ask` would load the embedding model mid-question. Say the word and I'll run it now that nothing else is competing for RAM.

body.text:
Read the roadmap and DESKTOP.md. Here's the actual state, and one stale entry worth correcting.

## What the plan says is next

**Tier 3 — desktop app (owner-promoted, NOW ACTIVE)** is the only thing with an explicitly queued next increment. Steps 1–4 are all done: squash-merge fold, the read-only branch/diff API, the branch + diff UI, the Electron shell, and the token-gated action endpoints + panel. DESKTOP.md §5 step 4 ends by naming what's left, in these words:

> *Annotate, relink and reconcile are served but have no UI yet: annotate wants a real form and the repair verbs belong on attention items (§3 item 4's "guided repair"), which is the next increment, not this one.*

Then step 5, packaging (electron-builder config is checked in with a **placeholder appId**) — which bumps into your own gate: the public name must be decided before any public artifact.

**Tier 0 (indexing perf — your "not customer-viable" flag)** is in much better shape than the doc admits. The chosen path shipped: DirectML on the 3060 took reindex from ~30 min to 78s (`2c37dc6`). The ROADMAP still calls it "in progress" — that's stale, and I'd fix it in a one-line edit. What genuinely remains there:

- **#4 over-invalidation** — an incremental run re-embedded ~494 chunks for only ~26 cache hits after 8 commits. That reuse rate still looks wrong, and it's a measurement task before it's a fix. Cheap, and it makes every future run cheaper.
- **#2 smaller/faster model** — folds into Tier 1's retrieval-quality eval rather than standing alone.
- **#3 ORT memory bounding** — mostly addressed by batching + the exit guard; the per-batch watchdog is the leftover.

**Tier 1 hardening**, roughly by leverage: capture enrichment (mine `reasoning.tested` from transcript spans into auto-captured entries — small, self-contained, and it compounds because every future commit records more); retrieval-quality eval (the embedder was chosen for the offline promise, never measured); read-perf beyond `report` (`log --intent` and `doctor` still resolve identity per commit); fix or delete the permanently-red lint gate.

**Tier 2** is the one that isn't polish: **dogfood on a real external project**. The roadmap's own framing — a codebase that doesn't know about the tool — is where capture-adapter and scale problems surface that nothing internal will find.

## My recommendation

Finish the desktop increment the plan already queued: **the annotate form + attention-item guided repair**. It's the smallest well-specified piece of work on the board, it closes the gap where three verbs are served by the API but unreachable in the UI, and it's what makes the app usable in anger rather than merely launchable. Packaging then sits behind one decision only you can make (the name).

If you'd rather spend the next session on leverage than completion, **Tier 2's external dogfood** is the higher-information move — it's the only item that can invalidate assumptions rather than confirm them. Everything in Tier 1 will still be there afterward, and some of it may turn out not to matter.

Want me to fix the stale Tier 0 entry now, and start on the annotate form?

python - <<'PY'
p='architecture/ROADMAP.md'
s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
s=s.replace("**SHIPPED 2026-07-24**\n   (`2c37dc6`)","**SHIPPED 2026-07-19**\n   (`2c37dc6`)",1)
old="""worse odds. This tier gates customer-facing ambitions."""
new="""worse odds. This tier gates customer-facing ambitions.

**Status update 2026-07-25:** the gating item (GPU execution, #1 below) shipped the same
week — a full reindex of this repo is now **78 seconds**, down from ~30 minutes. The flag in
this heading is kept because it was recorded as a customer-viability judgement, not a
wall-time one, and the remaining items (#2–#4) are what a 10–100× larger repo would still
run into. On this machine, for this repo, indexing is no longer the bottleneck it was."""
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8',newline='').write(s)
print('ok')
PY
sed -n '12,50p' architecture/ROADMAP.md

git add architecture/ROADMAP.md && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Roadmap said the GPU work was in progress; it shipped a week ago

Tier 0's gating item (DirectML on the local GPU) landed in 2c37dc6 on 2026-07-19 and
took a full reindex of this repo from ~30 minutes to 78 seconds, but the roadmap still
described it as "in progress" — so anyone reading the plan, human or agent, would have
mis-ranked what is actually left.

Marked shipped with the measured number, and added a status note under the tier heading
rather than deleting the "not customer-viable as is" flag: that flag was recorded as a
customer-viability judgement about repos 10-100x this size, not a wall-time one about
this machine, and items 2-4 (model size, ORT memory bounding, over-invalidation) are
still what a large repo would hit. Removing it would overclaim; leaving it unqualified
would misinform.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
